claim: Seasonal migration allows animals to cope with temporal environmental fluctuations by moving between geographically distant habitats.
source: Seasonal migration allows animals to cope with temporal environmental fluctuations by moving between geographically distant habitats (Fryxell and Sinclair, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fryxell and Sinclair, 1988

claim: Migration has evolved repeatedly in many taxa.
source: Given that much of our planet offers seasonally varying resources, it is not surprising that migration has evolved repeatedly in many taxa (Chapman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chapman et al., 2011

claim: Migration should offer either survival or breeding benefits compared to residency.
source: Theoretical research on the evolution of migration (Lundberg, 1987; 1988; Taylor and Norris, 2007; Griswold et al., 2010; Kokko, 2011; Shaw and Levin, 2011; Shaw and Couzin, 2013) has yielded a key prediction: migration should offer either survival or breeding benefits compared to residency.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to theoretical research

claim: Female migrant steelheads have higher fecundity than females that remain in fresh water streams.
source: Recent comparisons of migrant and resident steelheads (Oncorhynchus mykiss) found that female migrants have higher fecundity than females that remain in fresh water streams (Satterthwaite et al., 2009; Hodge et al., 2014, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on steelheads

claim: The noctuid moth performs a multi-generational migration which confers substantial reproductive benefits by allowing a lineage to spread to multiple sites.
source: Similarly, the noctuid moth (Autographa gamma) performs a multi-generational migration which confer substantial reproductive benefits by allowing a lineage to spread to multiple sites (Chapman et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chapman et al., 2012

claim: Individuals of Rutilus rutilus increase their survival during the winter by migrating from lakes to streams to avoid predation risks.
source: Regarding survival benefits, individuals of a fresh water fish (Rutilus rutilus), increase their survival during the winter by migrating from lakes to streams to avoid predation risks (Skov et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Skov et al., 2013

claim: Seasonal migration in birds allows individuals to avoid inhospitable conditions during the non-breeding season while the same region can offer abundant resources during the breeding season.
source: In birds, seasonal migration has often been argued to bring about survival benefits, as it allows individuals to avoid inhospitable conditions during the non-breeding season, while the same region can offer abundant resources during the breeding season (Lack, 1954).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lack, 1954

claim: If residency enhances breeding success in territorial birds, then there should be a corresponding benefit to migrants, with higher survival over non-breeding season being a clear possibility.
source: Theory predicts that if residency enhances breeding success in territorial birds, then there should be a corresponding benefit to migrants; higher survival over non-breeding season is a clear, but empirically understudied, possibility (Lundberg, 1987; Kokko, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical models

claim: There is limited empirical evidence regarding fitness benefits of bird migration.
source: Despite the extensive research done on bird migration, there is limited empirical evidence regarding its fitness benefits, as data on fitness-related variation in migratory strategies are logistically difficult to collect in the field.
evidence: Statement about the state of empirical evidence in the field

claim: Migrant European robins have lower survival and reproductive success than residents.
source: Despite logistical challenges, studies on European robins (Erithacus rubecula) and American dippers (Cinclus mexicanus) report that migrants have lower survival and reproductive success than residents (Adriaensen and Dhondt, 1990; Gillis et al., 2008; Green et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies

claim: Migrant American dippers have lower survival and reproductive success than residents.
source: Despite logistical challenges, studies on European robins (Erithacus rubecula) and American dippers (Cinclus mexicanus) report that migrants have lower survival and reproductive success than residents (Adriaensen and Dhondt, 1990; Gillis et al., 2008; Green et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies

claim: Resident cormorants have higher reproductive success than migrant cormorants.
source: Further, a recent study comparing fitness measures of resident and migrant cormorants (Phalacrocorax aristotelis) reported higher reproductive success in residents compared to migrants (Grist et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grist et al., 2017

claim: The migrants of the studied blackbird population overwinter, on average, 800 km west-southwest from the breeding grounds.
source: The migrants of our population overwinter, on average, 800 km west-southwest from the breeding grounds (Fudickar and Partecke, 2012) (Figure 2a and b)
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figure 2a and b showing overwintering locations

claim: The majority of migrants in the studied blackbird population are females.
source: the majority of migrants are females (Fudickar et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fudickar et al., 2013

claim: Multi-event survival models were fitted using presence-absence data obtained by capture-mark-recapture and radio-telemetry of 192 resident and 70 migrant free-living blackbirds over seven years.
source: We fitted multi-event survival models using presence-absence data obtained by capture-mark-recapture and radio-telemetry of 192 resident and 70 migrant free-living blackbirds over the course of seven years.
evidence: Description of the study methodology and sample sizes

claim: Multi-event survival models account for variation in re-encounter probabilities in relation to space, time and behaviour of the birds.
source: These models account for variation in re-encounter probabilities in relation to space, time and behaviour of the birds.
evidence: Description of the statistical model capabilities

claim: Migrants and residents of the breeding population are in sympatry during the summer months (March - October).
source: Migrants and residents of a breeding population of European blackbirds are in sympatry during the summer months (March - October).
evidence: Stated in Figure 1 caption

claim: During the wintering months (November – March) migrants and residents overwinter in different habitats.
source: During the wintering months (November – March) migrants and residents overwinter in different habitats.
evidence: Stated in Figure 1 caption

claim: Blackbirds had lower probability to survive the winter (Φ = 0.60; 95% CI = 0.55–0.66) than the summer season (Φ = 0.89; 95% CI = 0.82–0.94).
source: We found that winter mortality is an important determinant of lifespan, as blackbirds had lower probability to survive the winter (Φ = 0.60; 95% CI = 0.55–0.66) than the summer season (Φ = 0.89; 95% CI = 0.82–0.94) (Table 1, model 3)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis results presented in Table 1, model 3

claim: Winter mortality is an important determinant of lifespan in blackbirds.
source: We found that winter mortality is an important determinant of lifespan, as blackbirds had lower probability to survive the winter (Φ = 0.60; 95% CI = 0.55–0.66) than the summer season (Φ = 0.89; 95% CI = 0.82–0.94) (Table 1, model 3)
evidence: Inferred from the lower winter survival probability compared to summer

claim: The result that blackbirds have lower winter survival strongly supports the hypothesis that migration confers survival benefits compared with residency.
source: This result strongly supports the hypothesis that migration confers survival benefits compared with residency as an alternative strategy.
evidence: Inference drawn from the survival data analysis

claim: There was no difference between juveniles and adults in survival probability within a season.
source: There was no difference between juveniles and adults in survival probability within a season.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis results

claim: Juveniles have similar probability to survive the summer (Φ = 0.89; 95% CI = 0.80–0.94) as adults (Φ = 0.90; 95% CI = 0.83–0.94).
source: Juveniles (Φ = 0.89; 95% CI = 0.80–0.94; model 4 Table 1) have similar probability to survive the summer as adults (Φ = 0.90; 95% CI = 0.83–0.94; model 4 Table 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis results in model 4, Table 1

claim: During winter, juveniles have a comparable probability (Φ = 0.59; 95% CI = 0.49–0.68) to survive as adults (Φ = 0.61; 95% CI = 0.55–0.67).
source: During winter, juveniles also have a comparable probability (Φ = 0.59; 95% CI = 0.49–0.68; model 4 Table 1) to survive as adults (Φ = 0.61; 95% CI = 0.55–0.67; model 4 Table 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis results in model 4, Table 1

claim: Migratory European blackbirds had higher winter survival rates than resident blackbirds.
source: In line with our predictions, migratory European blackbirds had higher winter survival rates than resident blackbirds.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis results

claim: The best model estimated markedly higher winter survival for migrants (Φ = 0.73; 95% CI = 0.62–0.81) than for residents (Φ = 0.57; 95% CI = 0.50–0.63).
source: The best model (model 1, Table 1) estimated markedly higher winter survival for migrants (Φ = 0.73; 95% confidence intervals (CI) = 0.62–0.81, Figure 3) than for residents (Φ = 0.57; 95% CI = 0.50–0.63, Figure 3)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis results from model 1 in Table 1 and shown in Figure 3

claim: Detection probability for migrants was lower (P=0.19; 95% CI = 0.13–0.26) compared to residents (P=0.74; 95% CI = 0.69–0.78).
source: taking into account the lower detection probability for migrants (P=0.19; 95% CI = 0.13–0.26, Figure 3) compared to residents (P=0.74; 95% CI = 0.69–0.78).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis results shown in Figure 3

claim: Model 2, which included sex, had modest support (delta AICc = 0.95).
source: Our second model, which included sex and had modest support (model 2, delta AICc = 0.95, Table 1)
evidence: Supported by model comparison statistics in Table 1

claim: Model 2 predicted that migrants have higher winter survival probability than residents.
source: predicted that migrants have higher winter survival probability than residents, which was also predicted by model 1.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis results from model 2

claim: Sex differences in survival were not substantial.
source: Sex differences were not substantial (during summer: male residents Φ = 0.90; 95% CI = 0.83–0.95; female residents Φ = 0.89; 95% CI = 0.89–0.94; male migrants Φ = 0.95; 95% CI = 0.89–0.98, female migrants Φ = 0.94; 95% CI = 0.87–0.97; during winter: male residents Φ = 0.58; 95% CI = 0.51–0.65; female residents Φ = 0.53; 95% CI = 0.44–0.62; male migrants Φ = 0.75; 95% CI = 0.63–0.84, and female migrants Φ = 0.71; 95% CI = 0.60–0.81; detection probability was lower for migrants (P=0.19; 95% CI = 0.13–0.26) than for residents (P=0.74; 95% CI = 0.69–0.78)).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis results showing overlapping confidence intervals

claim: The findings support the theoretical predictions that migration yields survival benefits during the winter.
source: Our findings support the theoretical predictions that migration yields survival benefits during the winter.
evidence: Inference drawn from the survival data analysis

claim: The results provide an explanation for the maintenance of the migrant phenotype in the partially migratory population of European blackbirds.
source: In addition, our results provide an explanation for the maintenance of the migrant phenotype in the partially migratory population of European blackbirds that we studied.
evidence: Inference drawn from the survival data analysis

claim: Residency is predicted to provide reproductive benefits given that year-round occupancy provides advantages in establishing breeding territories.
source: Residency is predicted to provide reproductive benefits given that year-round occupancy provides, for example, advantages in establishing breeding territories (Kokko, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical model

claim: The two phenotypes (migrant and resident) can persist as evolutionary stable strategies (ESS) due to frequency dependent selection if the overall fitness of migrants and residents is equal.
source: The two phenotypes can persist as evolutionary stable strategies (ESS) due to frequency dependent selection if the overall fitness of migrants and residents is equal (Lundberg, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical model

claim: The expected lifetime number of reproductive seasons is 61.25% higher for migrants than for residents due to higher survival of the former.
source: Therefore, the expected lifetime number of reproductive seasons is 61.25% higher for migrants than for residents due to higher survival of the former.
evidence: Calculated from the survival probabilities using a mathematical model

claim: The reproductive performance of residents would have to be 61.25% higher than in migrants to achieve equal fitness of the alternative strategies.
source: We conclude from this calculation that the reproductive performance of residents would have to be 61.25% higher than in migrants to achieve equal fitness of the alternative strategies.
evidence: Calculated from the survival probabilities using a mathematical model

claim: Benefits to residents could come about from prior residency effects (either occupying a better territory or avoiding floater status), combined with a longer time spent in the breeding habitat which can make multiple nesting or re-nesting more likely.
source: Such benefits could come about from prior residency effects (either occupying a better territory or avoiding floater status), combined with a longer time spent in the breeding habitat which can make multiple nesting or re-nesting (in case of failure) more likely.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms

claim: Blackbirds are a multi-brood species (2–3 broods a year).
source: Considering that blackbirds are a multi-brood species (2–3 broods a year)
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about blackbird breeding biology

claim: It could be possible that residents gain a 61.25% higher breeding success compared to migrants.
source: it could be possible that residents gain a 61.25% higher breeding success compared to migrants.
evidence: Speculative statement based on breeding biology and calculated fitness requirements

claim: If resident breeding success is higher than 61.25%, then the fitness of migrants will be lower than the fitness of residents and migration would be a conditional strategy operating under frequency-dependent selection.
source: If resident breeding success is higher than 61.25%, then the fitness of migrants will be lower than the fitness of residents and migration would be a conditional strategy operating under frequency-dependent selection.
evidence: Logical inference from the fitness calculations

claim: For conditional migration strategies, some intrinsic phenotypic characteristics (sex, age, dominance) result in a need to adopt a strategy that might yield overall lower fitness than what residents on average achieve, but it is the better choice to optimize individual fitness.
source: For conditional migration strategies, some intrinsic phenotypic characteristics (sex, age, dominance) result in a need to adopt a strategy that might yield overall lower fitness than what residents on average achieve, but it is the better choice to optimize individual fitness (Lundberg, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical model

claim: Year-to-year variation of winter environmental conditions at the breeding grounds may play a role shaping the incidence of migration versus residency over time.
source: It is also plausible that year-to-year variation of winter environmental conditions at the breeding grounds play a role shaping the incidence of migration versus residency over time.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about environmental effects

claim: During a harsh and long winter, the survival of residents might be lower compared to a mild and short winter.
source: For instance, during a harsh and long winter, the survival of residents might be lower compared to a mild and short winter.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about environmental effects on survival

claim: If fewer residents survive an unusually harsh winter and establish breeding territories during the subsequent breeding season, many high-quality territories would remain vacant for migrants to take advantage of after arrival in the spring.
source: If fewer residents survive an unusually harsh winter and establish breeding territories during the subsequent breeding season, many high-quality territories would remain vacant for migrants to take advantage of after arrival in the spring.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about consequences of harsh winters

claim: If residents that do survive harsh winters begin the breeding season in poor condition, then physically dominant migrants could successfully take-over prime territories from residents.
source: Furthermore, if residents that do survive harsh winters begin the breeding season in poor condition, then physically dominant migrants could successfully take-over prime territories from residents.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about territory acquisition dynamics

claim: Under the scenario where migrants can take over territories from weakened residents, the prior residency effect would not be acting at full strength and migrants would gain breeding benefits.
source: Under this scenario, the prior residency effect would not be acting at full strength (Drent et al., 2003; Jahn et al., 2010; Kokko, 2011) and migrants would gain breeding benefits.
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citations

claim: There was no evidence for sex differences in survival.
source: We found no evidence for sex differences in survival (though some ambiguity remains, as a moderately supported model two includes sex as an explanatory variable — note that the best model does not).
evidence: Based on statistical model comparison results

claim: Females are more likely to migrate than males in the study population.
source: This raises the question: why are females more likely to migrate than males in the study population (Fudickar et al., 2013)?
evidence: Supported by citation to Fudickar et al., 2013

claim: Overwintering blackbirds form foraging flocks and an individual's access to food is related to its position within the flock hierarchy.
source: One line of thinking is to argue that residency is more dangerous for females than for males, because overwintering blackbirds form foraging flocks and an individual's access to food is related to its position within the flock hierarchy (Lundberg and Schwabl, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lundberg and Schwabl, 1983

claim: Within foraging flocks, females are subordinate to males.
source: Within these flocks, females are subordinate to males (Lundberg and Schwabl, 1983; Lundberg, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lundberg and Schwabl, 1983 and Lundberg, 1985

claim: The data do not align perfectly with the interpretation that residency is more dangerous for females than males due to subordinate status in flocks.
source: However, our data do not align perfectly with this interpretation: if overwinter survival during residency was a strong factor driving sex differences in migratory strategy, we ought to have seen lower winter survival in resident females than in males, but this was not the case.
evidence: Inference from the survival data analysis showing no sex difference

claim: Resident males may enjoy priority access to prime territories as soon as the breeding season starts.
source: It is conceivable that resident males enjoy priority access to prime territories as soon as the breeding season starts.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about territory acquisition

claim: Females may also benefit from better territories, thus an early presence may be beneficial for them as well.
source: However, it should always be remembered that females, too, may benefit from better territories, thus an early presence may be beneficial for them as well (Creighton, 2001; Kokko et al., 2006; Kokko, 2011; Snow, 1956).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Reproductive success of migrant and resident blackbirds is sex-dependent such that male residents have higher reproductive success than male migrants, while female residents and migrants have similar reproductive success.
source: It would be important to understand exactly how territory acquisition differs between males and females, especially because earlier data from the same geographical area have shown that reproductive success of migrant and resident blackbirds is sex-dependent (Schwabl, 1983) such that male residents have higher reproductive success than male migrants, while female residents and migrants have similar reproductive success.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwabl, 1983

claim: If frequency-dependency penalizes late-arriving males whereas late breeding females are not severely penalized, then the same magnitude of survival differences will favor a larger migratory population within females than within males.
source: Understanding the mechanisms of territory acquisition could help explain why fewer males migrate: if frequency-dependency penalizes late-arriving males whereas late breeding females are not severely penalized, then the same magnitude of survival differences will favor a larger migratory population within females than within males.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about sex-specific migration patterns
